    # that is not what origin/master holds would be waiting on the wrong build.
    # Rebasing is a history decision, so say what is wrong and stop.
    git -C "$repo" fetch --quiet origin master
    sha=$(git -C "$repo" rev-parse HEAD)
    remote=$(git -C "$repo" rev-parse origin/master)
    if [ "$sha" = "$remote" ]; then
      echo "hms: ''${sha:0:7} is already origin/master"
    elif git -C "$repo" merge-base --is-ancestor "$remote" "$sha"; then
      # Fetching narrows the race but cannot close it — another box can advance
      # origin/master between the fetch and the push. Catch that rather than let
      # `set -e` surface the same hint wall this block exists to avoid. git keeps
      # its stderr: a rejected push and a failed auth are not the same problem,
      # and only a ref that actually moved earns the race message.
      if git -C "$repo" push --quiet origin HEAD:master; then
        echo "hms: pushed ''${sha:0:7}"
      else
        # Only a ref we watched move earns the race message. An ls-remote that
        # did not run tells us nothing, and guessing "someone else pushed" from
        # its empty output would point at the wrong culprit.
        moved=""
        if now=$(git -C "$repo" ls-remote --heads origin master 2>/dev/null | cut -f1) \
           && [ -n "$now" ] && [ "$now" != "$remote" ]; then
          moved=1
        fi
        if [ -n "$moved" ]; then
          echo "hms: push lost the race — origin/master moved just now. Re-run." >&2
        else
          echo "hms: push failed — see git's error above." >&2
        fi
        exit 1
      fi
    else
      behind=$(git -C "$repo" rev-list --count "$sha..$remote")
      ahead=$(git -C "$repo" rev-list --count "$remote..$sha")
      echo "hms: origin/master (''${remote:0:7}) has $behind commit(s) you do not have." >&2
      if [ "$ahead" -gt 0 ]; then
        echo "hms: and you have $ahead it does not — rebase, then re-run." >&2
      else
        echo "hms: you are strictly behind — pull, then re-run." >&2
      fi
      # -n 5 rather than `| head -5`: under pipefail, head closing the pipe makes
      # git exit 141 and `set -e` aborts on that instead of the exit 1 below.
      git -C "$repo" --no-pager log --oneline -n 5 "$sha..$remote" >&2
      exit 1

content.content:
# `hms` — switch this host, but let the forge do the building.
  #
  # A local switch compiles whatever is not in attic; the in-cluster runner has
  # far more of everything and pushes its result to attic, so waiting for CI and
  # then switching turns the switch into a pure download. The wait is only worth
  # it because the closure CI pushes is bit-identical to the one we would build.
  #
  # Refuses on a dirty tree: CI builds a pushed commit, so an uncommitted switch
  # is one CI can never reproduce, and silently building it locally would hide
  # that. `--local` is the escape hatch for exactly that case.
  hms = pkgs.writeShellScriptBin "hms" ''
    set -euo pipefail

    repo="$HOME/devel/dotfiles"
    host="$(uname -n)"
    forge="https://forge.ko.ag"
    slug="sauyon/dotfiles"
    curl=${lib.getExe pkgs.curl}
    jq=${lib.getExe pkgs.jq}

    local_only=0
    hm_args=()
    for a in "$@"; do
      case "$a" in
        -l|--local) local_only=1 ;;
        -h|--help)
          echo "usage: hms [--local] [home-manager switch args...]"
          echo "  default: push HEAD, wait for its CI run, then switch (a download)"
          echo "  --local: skip CI and build here"
          exit 0 ;;
        *) hm_args+=("$a") ;;
      esac
    done

    switch_now() {
      exec home-manager switch --flake "$repo#$host" ''${hm_args[@]+"''${hm_args[@]}"}
    }

    # mari (darwin) has no Linux CI job; nix-home.yml builds only these.
    case "$host" in
      utsuho|setsuna|fujiwara|shiori) ;;
      *) echo "hms: $host has no CI job — switching locally" >&2; switch_now ;;
    esac

    [ "$local_only" -eq 0 ] || switch_now

cdb6ee06d77fc0a15032082b5cf93cdbb32ca8b1
sops: add the offline paper recipient for the dotfiles secrets

Report A7 step 1, the last prerequisite the A7 migration gate names that
was not a host enrollment. `secrets.yaml` now has a fourth way in that
needs no Google account, no network and no machine: an age recipient
whose private half exists only on paper.

It goes in the SAME creation rule as gcp_kms, so sops keeps all three in
one key group and any ONE of them decrypts. `key_groups` would have been
the wrong shape -- that is a Shamir AND, and a paper key that needs a
second share is not a recovery path. The comment in .sops.yaml says so,
because the shape is invisible once the file is encrypted.

`sops updatekeys` ran on fujiwara under the human's ADC (the only
identity holding encrypt on both KMS keys; shiori's device identity has
decrypt on host-key and nothing else, so it structurally cannot do this).
The data key is unchanged -- `mac` did not move and no ENC[] payload line
is in the diff -- so this re-wraps the existing key for a new recipient
rather than re-encrypting any secret.

Four decrypt paths checked against this exact file, because the risk here
is silently breaking one of the three that already worked:

  - the paper identity alone, every Google credential stripped and
    CLOUDSDK_CONFIG pointed at an empty directory so gcloud's ADC cannot
    quietly do the work  (tests/sops-recipients.sh)
  - shiori's device WIF identity -> STS -> host-key                 (sops -d)

wif: cases for a TPM-resident device key (red)

Part A item 2. Written and watched fail before any of the code it
covers existed, on shiori with its TPM present:

  FAIL 1 - the device key exists and is TPM-resident
  ok   2 - the plain file-key path still signs and verifies ...
  FAIL 3 - shiori's credential config signs with .../wif-tpm.pem
           it names: --key /home/sauyon/.config/ko/wif.pem
  FAIL 4 - ko-wif-token exports OPENSSL_MODULES and TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI

Check 2 passing at that point is the shape of the task: the file-key
path is the invariant, not the deliverable. mari is darwin with no TPM
and the other four hosts are unenrolled, so it stays the path most of
the fleet boots on, and it is exercised with no provider environment at
all -- the darwin case, reproduced.

The check the whole item rests on is the negative one. "The key is in
the TPM" is not observable from a file that claims to be a TPM blob, so
the test points TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI at /dev/null -- a character device that
is not a TPM -- and REQUIRES the signature to fail. A key whose private
half were still on disk would sign there and pass everything else.

The signature round trip re-derives DER from the JWS raw r||s here
rather than reusing the signer's own der_sig_to_raw: a bug those two
shared would verify against itself and prove nothing.

git add home.nix home/scripts/ko-wif-token.py install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
wif: move shiori's device key into the TPM

Part A item 2 (report A1 #1, A6.5). ~/.config/ko/wif.pem was a P-256
private key in plaintext on disk: one read of it mints device JWTs
forever, from anywhere, and the KMS access log cannot tell that from
shiori. The new key is a TSS2 blob wrapped to this TPM's owner
hierarchy -- copy the file elsewhere and it signs nothing.

Mechanism: the nixpkgs tpm2-openssl PROVIDER, not tpm2-pkcs11. Both
would work, and the choice was mine to make, so the reasons: the
provider needs two exports in the ko-wif-token wrapper and nothing else
-- no token database, no init step, no PIN -- and it keeps the signer
on stdlib + openssl, which is the constraint that made this script a
python file instead of a Go binary. Measured on shiori: genpkey writes
the blob, `pkey -pubout` yields the same SubjectPublicKeyInfo shape the
JWK code already parses, and `dgst -sha256 -sign` takes 0.18s.

The signer decides per key, by sniffing the PEM header, rather than
taking a flag. A flag would have to be threaded through the credential
config, device-test.sh and every interactive invocation in the same
commit, and a host whose key moved into the TPM would break at whichever
one was missed. key_args also names `default` a second time, because
naming any provider switches the implicit one off and takes the digest
and the encoders with it.

`ec` -> `pkey` for the public half: `ec` is the legacy EC-only command
and the TPM key comes out of the provider's generic store loader. The
file-key path is unchanged by it -- shiori's file key still produces kid
REDACTED, the one in the published
JWKS.

wifTpmHosts is a separate list from wifHosts because it is a separate
fact: enrolment (a published JWK) and where the private half lives are
independent, and mari is darwin with no TPM at all. Listing a host there
before its JWK is in the bucket earns it an STS 401 at the next
activation -- publish first, switch second, which is what tpm-keygen.sh
prints at the end.

tpm-keygen.sh refuses to overwrite an existing key. Silently rotating is
how a host stops matching its published JWK: old kid in the JWKS, new
key signing, 401 with nothing local to explain it. It also sign-verifies
the new blob through the TPM before installing it, so a key the chip
will not load is found now rather than at the next boot inside
sops-install-secrets.

No PCR policy and no auth value, deliberately: sops-nix decrypts
unattended at activation and at boot, so a passphrase or a boot
measurement would turn a kernel update into a host that cannot read its
own secrets. The cost is that anyone with code execution as this user
can ask the TPM to sign -- the TPM buys non-exportability, not
unattended-use protection. A TPM clear is a re-enrolment, not a
recovery.

  ./tests/wif-tpm.sh   8 checks, all good

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git log --oneline -3; git status --short

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Device side. Generates a TPM-RESIDENT P-256 device WIF key (report A1 #1, A6.5,
# Part A item 2) and prints its public JWK for the admin machine.
#
# The file this writes is not a private key: it is a TPM key blob, wrapped to a
# primary under this TPM's owner hierarchy. Copy it to another machine and it
# signs nothing. That is the entire upgrade over device-keygen.sh, whose
# ~/.config/ko/wif.pem is a plain P-256 private key that anyone who reads it once
# can use forever, from anywhere, indistinguishably from this host.
#
#   ./install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh [path]     # default: ~/.config/ko/wif-tpm.pem
#
# What it does NOT survive:
#   * a TPM clear (firmware setup, some BIOS updates, `tpm2_clear`) -- the owner
#     seed changes and the blob becomes undecryptable. That is a re-enrolment,
#     not a recovery: run this again and publish the new JWK.
#   * a motherboard swap, for the same reason.
# Both are fine as long as another recipient of secrets.yaml still works, which
# is what the paper key and (until the item 4 gate) nix-key are for.
#
# No PCR policy and no auth value: sops-nix decrypts unattended at activation and
# at boot, so anything that needs a passphrase or a matching boot measurement
# turns a kernel update into a host that cannot read its own secrets.
set -euo pipefail

out="${1:-${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/ko/wif-tpm.pem}"
here="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
repo="$(cd "$here/../.." && pwd)"
host="$(uname -n)"; host="${host%%.*}"
tcti="${TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI:-device:/dev/tpmrm0}"

# The repo is public, and a TPM blob is still a credential in the sense that
# matters here: committing one advertises the host's enrolment.
case "$(realpath -m "$out")" in
  "$repo"/*) echo "refusing to write the device key inside the repo: $out" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
if [ -e "$out" ]; then
  # Overwriting is how a host silently stops matching its published JWK: the old
  # kid stays in the JWKS, the new key signs, and STS returns 401 with nothing
  # local to explain it.
  echo "exists, refusing to overwrite: $out" >&2
  echo "to rotate, move it aside, run this again, and republish the JWKS with the new JWK" >&2
  exit 1
fi

dev="${tcti#device:}"
if [ ! -e "$dev" ]; then
  echo "no TPM at $dev (set TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI to point elsewhere)" >&2; exit 1
fi
if [ ! -w "$dev" ]; then
  echo "$dev is not writable by $(id -un); on Arch that means joining the 'tss' group" >&2; exit 1
fi

# openssl and the tpm2 provider must come from ONE source: a provider built
# against a different OpenSSL than the binary loading it fails to load, and the
# error names neither. This flake's pkgs first, because that is the pair home.nix
# wires into ko-wif-token, so a key made here is made by the tools that will use
# it; nixpkgs as the fallback for a checkout that cannot evaluate.
pick() { # pick <relative path> <flake attr>... -> first out path that contains it
  local p attr
  for attr in "${@:2}"; do
    for p in $(nix build --no-link --print-out-paths "$attr" 2>/dev/null); do
      [ -e "$p/$1" ] && { printf '%s\n' "$p"; return 0; }
    done
  done
  return 1
}
ossl_root=$(pick bin/openssl ".#homeConfigurations.$host.pkgs.openssl" "nixpkgs#openssl") \
  || { echo "need openssl (nixpkgs#openssl)" >&2; exit 1; }
prov_root=$(pick lib/ossl-modules/tpm2.so ".#homeConfigurations.$host.pkgs.tpm2-openssl" "nixpkgs#tpm2-openssl") \
  || { echo "need the tpm2 openssl provider (nixpkgs#tpm2-openssl)" >&2; exit 1; }
OSSL="$ossl_root/bin/openssl"
export OPENSSL_MODULES="$prov_root/lib/ossl-modules"
export TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI="$tcti"

dir="$(dirname "$out")"
mkdir -p "$dir"; chmod 700 "$dir"
umask 077
# Beside $out so the final mv stays on one filesystem: the key appears whole or
# not at all, and a half-written blob is indistinguishable from a wrong one.
tmpd="$(mktemp -d "$dir/.tpm-keygen.XXXXXX")"
trap 'rm -rf "$tmpd"' EXIT

if ! err="$("$OSSL" genpkey -provider tpm2 -provider default \
              -algorithm EC -pkeyopt group:P-256 -out "$tmpd/key" 2>&1)"; then
  printf '%s\n' "openssl genpkey (tpm2) failed: $err" >&2; exit 1
fi
head -1 "$tmpd/key" | grep -qx -- '-----BEGIN TSS2 PRIVATE KEY-----' || {
  echo "openssl wrote $(head -1 "$tmpd/key") -- that is not a TPM key blob; refusing it" >&2
  exit 1
}

# Prove the key signs through the TPM before installing it. A blob the chip will
# not load is worth finding now, not at the next boot in sops-install-secrets.
printf 'tpm-keygen self test' > "$tmpd/msg"
"$OSSL" dgst -sha256 -sign "$tmpd/key" -provider tpm2 -provider default \
  -out "$tmpd/sig" "$tmpd/msg" 2>/dev/null \
  && "$OSSL" pkey -provider tpm2 -provider default -in "$tmpd/key" -pubout -out "$tmpd/pub.pem" 2>/dev/null \
  && "$OSSL" dgst -sha256 -verify "$tmpd/pub.pem" -signature "$tmpd/sig" "$tmpd/msg" >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  || { echo "the new key could not sign-and-verify through the TPM; not installing it" >&2; exit 1; }

chmod 400 "$tmpd/key"
mv "$tmpd/key" "$out"

mkdir -p "$here/out"
jwk="$here/out/$host-tpm.jwk.json"
KO_OPENSSL="$OSSL" python3 "$repo/home/scripts/ko-wif-token.py" --key "$out" --jwk | tee "$jwk"

echo
echo "wrote $out (mode 400, TPM-wrapped) and $jwk"
echo
echo "Next:"
echo "  1. carry ONLY $jwk to the admin machine (it is public)"
echo "  2. republish the JWKS with EVERY current key, this one included --"
echo "     admin-setup.sh replaces the JWKS with exactly the JWKs you pass it"
echo "  3. add $host to wifTpmHosts in home.nix, then build and switch (hms)"
echo "  4. ./tests/wif-tpm.sh $out"
echo
echo "Keep the old key published until the new generation is live: removing its"
echo "kid revokes the identity the RUNNING generation still signs with."

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/code-review

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions. The first names its addressee; the rest hold for anyone.

- **Never run a reviewer in the background — you, the agent in a herdr pane,
  where ending a turn *is* how you report done.** Do not set
  `run_in_background`, do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is
  out. A backgrounded reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a
  finished turn, and the run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it
  blocking and read its verdict in the turn you dispatched it. That reason is
  role-specific, so there is exactly one role it does not bind: the **driver**,
  which backgrounds the panel and ends the turn because its harness re-invokes
  it on process exit — `skills/pipeline/SKILL.md` says so at its own loop. A
  split by role, not a preference. In a pane, the prohibition is yours.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path, then classify the round by how the panel exited:

   | Exit | What it means |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | clean — a real range was reviewed, nothing blocking |
   | 3 | blocking findings; go to step 5 |
   | 2 | timeout — reviewers are slow, not broken. Re-run the same command: it resumes the panel in flight |
   | 1 | error, or an empty `<base>..HEAD` it refused. Fix the range or the setup; never re-run blindly |
   | 137/143 | **your own harness killed it.** drovr produced no verdict at all, and none of the rows above describes the run. Re-run to resume, and record the round as **unclassifiable** — never as a timeout |

   A reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the five: re-dispatch rather
   than report its silence.

   **Only 0 is clean, and one clean round does not end the loop.** Stop at
   whichever of three comes first:
   - **Two consecutive clean rounds over an unchanged HEAD.** Any edit between
     them resets the count — the second round is evidence about the first only
     if it read the same code.
   - **A cap of six rounds**, which is *not* a clean ending: write up every
     round's verdict and everything still open (step 5), and finish on that
     record rather than on a verdict. Only rounds that delivered every
     configured angle count toward the cap — a missing angle is a Critical
     stand-in, so a round that lost a reviewer never measured the code.
   - **Two consecutive rounds that lost a dimension** — its own outcome,
     neither clean nor the cap: the panel is failing to deliver and further
     rounds are not measuring the code. Name the angles that never ran. Without
     this the loop cannot end at all, since such a round is never clean and
     never counts toward the cap.

   Three caveats the rule owes you. Two cleans make a false clean **less
   likely**, not unlikely, and prove nothing about convergence — in forge#88's
   own data two consecutive cleans preceded a `changes` round with seven
   findings. **Six is a starting number, revisable on evidence**, not a
   principled constant. And every word of this is prose nothing enforces — the
   shape of the *"re-run it"* that produced 47 re-arms over 14 hours.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral with
   `drovr code-review defer`.** Per finding: quote it, then name the edit
   answering it by file — or, if you are not making it, run

   ```
   drovr code-review defer <RUN> <TASK> --file <path> [--line <n>] \
     --severity <critical|important|nit> --summary "<the finding>" \
     --reason "<why it is not being fixed>"
   ```

   A deferral written only in prose is one the next round cannot read, so it
   re-raises the finding you already ruled on. The command appends to a
   per-task log every later seed carries; prose does not.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`. **Done is
   step 3's termination rule met, not the first exit 0** — say which of the
   three ended it, and on the cap or a lost dimension say plainly that the loop
   ended on a record rather than on a clean verdict.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

One read away, in `skills/code-review/worked-example.md`: a 320-line spec, a
client call in 19 minutes, a $45,000 sign-off and a lead writing *"just send
it"* — the rationalization refused, the panel run, two Importants found, the
call moved 22 minutes. Worth reading once; the rules above do not depend on it.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.
- `drovr:pipeline` — the driver's side of both split rules: it backgrounds the
  panel, and it runs step 3's termination rule from the loop's end.

Part A item 2 of a secrets trust-root migration: move the host "shiori"'s device Workload-Identity-Federation signing key from a plaintext P-256 file (~/.config/ko/wif.pem) into the TPM, using the nixpkgs tpm2-openssl PROVIDER. The key signs a 5-minute ES256 JWT; Google STS validates it against a JWKS published in a GCS bucket; the resulting federated token decrypts secrets via KMS. sops-nix runs the signer from a systemd user unit with PATH="" — every tool path must be absolute or come from the wrapper's exports.

- The plain file-key path must keep working unchanged for macOS (host "mari") and four not-yet-enrolled hosts. Those have no TPM and no tpm2-openssl.

What happens on a key file whose first line is not a PEM header, an empty file, a directory, a symlink, a very long first line? Does the file get read twice / could it change between reads? Is the openssl `ec`->`pkey` switch a silent behaviour change for any existing caller (check install/wif/device-keygen.sh, install/wif/device-test.sh, home.nix, tests/)?

Is passing `-provider` AFTER `-sign <key>` actually honoured by openssl's dgst, or is the key loaded before the providers are registered? If it works, does it work by accident? Verify by reasoning about the command line, and if you can, by running the real thing read-only (a scratch TPM key exists at ~/.config/ko/wif-tpm.pem; openssl is at /nix/store/44gxi8li8y8wrxrb93sya9hljkpigsqw-openssl-3.6.4-bin/bin/openssl, provider dir /nix/store/REDACTED.3.0/lib/ossl-modules, TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI=device:/dev/tpmrm0). Do NOT create, modify or delete any file; write scratch output only under /tmp/claude-1000 if you must.
3. home.nix: `wifTpmHosts`/`useWifTpm`/`wifKeyFile`. Is the darwin guard right? Could a host end up with the TPM key path but no provider exports, or vice versa? Is `pkgs.tpm2-openssl` guaranteed to be built against the same `pkgs.openssl` the wrapper exports as KO_OPENSSL? What happens on the four Linux hosts NOT in wifTpmHosts (utsuho/setsuna/fujiwara) — does anything change for them? Read the surrounding sops/wif block (home.nix lines ~28-95 and ~1470-1510).
4. tests/wif-tpm.sh: does each check actually exercise what its name claims, and would it FAIL on a regression? Be specific about: the `TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI=device:/dev/null` negative check (could it pass for the wrong reason — e.g. failing for an unrelated error rather than because the key is TPM-bound?); the raw-r||s -> DER conversion; the `tail -c 64` public-point extraction; the `unset OPENSSL_MODULES TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI` before the file-key check (does it really unset for the python child?); the `nix eval`/`nix build` wiring check; `pick()` using unquoted command substitution in a for loop; whether any check silently SKIPs on the very condition it is supposed to catch.
5. install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh: the refuse-to-overwrite, the repo-path guard, `mktemp -d` + `mv` atomicity, `chmod 400` before `mv`, the self-test, the `trap`, and whether a failure leaves a half-enrolled state. Does `pick()` handle a `nix build` that prints multiple output paths?
6. Anything where the TEST and the CODE share a bug and would agree with each other.

Also state explicitly whether the tests exercise the behaviour or merely pass.

OUTPUT: a list of findings, each with severity exactly one of Critical / Important / nit, plus file:line and a concrete failure scenario (inputs/state -> wrong behaviour). If you find none at a severity, say so explicitly. Do not soften: this is the last review before the change goes onto a live machine.

SP=/tmp/claude-1000/-home-sauyon-devel-dotfiles--drovr-wt-wif-enroll/4e777609-87db-4d8b-bcd5-8d279ae59f5e/scratchpad
cat > "$SP/2a-removal.sh" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Experiment 2a-removal (report A8): publish a JWKS with shiori's OLD file-key kid
# removed, then time how long STS keeps accepting a JWT signed by that old key.
# Run AFTER the new generation is live, so the removal revokes a key nothing uses.
set -uo pipefail
SP="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
REPO=/home/sauyon/devel/dotfiles/.drovr/wt/wif-enroll
REDACTED
ISS="https://storage.googleapis.com/ko-keys-sauyon/hosts"
AUD="//iam.googleapis.com/projects/484956590837/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/ko-hosts/providers/bucket"

curl -fsS --max-time 20 "$ISS/.well-known/jwks.json" -o "$SP/jwks-before.json" || exit 1
python3 - "$SP/jwks-before.json" "$OLD_KID" "$SP/jwks-after.json" <<'PY'
import json, sys
j = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
before = [k["kid"] for k in j["keys"]]
j["keys"] = [k for k in j["keys"] if k["kid"] != sys.argv[2]]
assert len(j["keys"]) == len(before) - 1, f"old kid not present: {before}"
json.dump(j, open(sys.argv[3], "w"), separators=(",", ":"))
print("before:", before)
print("after: ", [k["kid"] for k in j["keys"]])
PY
[ $? -eq 0 ] || exit 1

RD=$(ssh -o BatchMode=yes 10.0.7.100 'mktemp -d ~/.jwks-publish.XXXXXX') || exit 1
scp -q "$SP/jwks-after.json" "10.0.7.100:$RD/jwks.json" || exit 1
ssh -o BatchMode=yes 10.0.7.100 "export PATH=/nix/var/nix/profiles/default/bin:\$PATH
  nix shell nixpkgs#google-cloud-sdk -c gcloud storage cp --content-type=application/json \
    --cache-control='public, max-age=60' '$RD/jwks.json' gs://ko-keys-sauyon/hosts/.well-known/jwks.json" || exit 1
start=$(date +%s)
ssh -o BatchMode=yes 10.0.7.100 "rm -rf '$RD'"
echo "== removed $OLD_KID at $(date -u +%H:%M:%SZ); timing until STS rejects it =="

# Sign with the OLD FILE key -- the point is to watch a removed kid stop working.
for i in $(seq 1 120); do
  umask 077
  python3 "$REPO/home/scripts/ko-wif-token.py" --key "$HOME/.config/ko/wif.pem" \
    --iss "$ISS" --sub device:shiori --aud "$AUD" > "$SP/old.jwt" 2>/dev/null || { echo "sign failed"; break; }
  code=$(curl -sS -o "$SP/sts.json" -w '%{http_code}' https://sts.googleapis.com/v1/token \
    --data-urlencode grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange \
    --data-urlencode "audience=$AUD" \
    --data-urlencode scope=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
    --data-urlencode requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token \
    --data-urlencode subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:jwt \
    --data-urlencode "subject_token@$SP/old.jwt")
  t=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))
  if [ "$code" != 200 ]; then
    echo "REJECTED after ${t}s (attempt $i, http $code): $(python3 -c 'import json,sys; d=json.load(open(sys.argv[1])); print(d.get("error"),"-",str(d.get("error_description"))[:100])' "$SP/sts.json" 2>/dev/null)"
    break
  fi
  echo "  t+${t}s: still accepted"
  sleep 10
done
rm -f "$SP/old.jwt"
echo "== new key still works? =="
python3 "$REPO/home/scripts/ko-wif-token.py" --key "$HOME/.config/ko/wif-tpm.pem" \
  --iss "$ISS" --sub device:shiori --aud "$AUD" > "$SP/new.jwt" 2>/dev/null
c=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://sts.googleapis.com/v1/token \
  --data-urlencode grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange \
  --data-urlencode "audience=$AUD" --data-urlencode scope=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
  --data-urlencode requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token \
  --data-urlencode subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:jwt \
  --data-urlencode "subject_token@$SP/new.jwt")
rm -f "$SP/new.jwt"
echo "TPM key -> STS http $c (200 expected)"
EOF
chmod +x "$SP/2a-removal.sh"; echo "prepared: $SP/2a-removal.sh"; bash -n "$SP/2a-removal.sh" && echo "syntax ok"

cat > ~/.local/share/drovr/runs/wif-enroll/task2-report.md <<'EOF'
# Task 2 report — shiori's device WIF key into the TPM (Part A item 2)

Base `5f671bb` (recorded in `task-2-base.sha` before the first edit).
Branch `drovr/wif-enroll` in `/home/sauyon/devel/dotfiles/.drovr/wt/wif-enroll`.

## What changed

Four files; `git diff 5f671bb..HEAD` is 409 insertions across them.

**`install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh` (new, +126)** — device-side generator for a
TPM-resident P-256 key.

    ./install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh [path]      # default ~/.config/ko/wif-tpm.pem
        # stdout: the public JWK, then the path written and the next steps.
        # also writes install/wif/out/<host>-tpm.jwk.json (that dir is gitignored).
        # exit 1: path inside the repo · path exists · no TPM at the TCTI device ·
        #         device not writable (tss group) · openssl/provider not resolvable ·
        #         genpkey produced something that is not a TSS2 blob ·
        #         the new key failed its sign-and-verify self test through the TPM.

**`home/scripts/ko-wif-token.py` (+39/-8)** — one new function, two call sites.

    def key_args(key) -> list[str]
        # ["-provider", "tpm2", "-provider", "default"] when the key file's first
        # line contains b"TSS2 PRIVATE KEY", else []. SystemExit on an unreadable file.

  `pub_xy` now runs `openssl pkey *key_args(key) -in KEY -pubout -outform DER`
  (was `openssl ec ...`); `sign` runs `openssl dgst -sha256 -sign KEY *key_args(key)`.
  The public CLI is unchanged: `--key/--jwk/--iss/--sub/--aud/--exp/--adc/--skip-clock-check`.
  `pub_xy`'s bad-point path now raises `SystemExit` rather than `ValueError`, so a
  wrong-curve key prints a message instead of a traceback.

**`home.nix` (+22/-2)** — three new let-bindings in the sops trust-root block and
two conditional exports in the `ko-wif-token` wrapper.

    wifTpmHosts = [ "shiori" ];
    useWifTpm   = useWif && !isDarwin && builtins.elem hostname wifTpmHosts;
    wifKeyFile  = "${config.home.homeDirectory}/.config/ko/"
                + (if useWifTpm then "wif-tpm.pem" else "wif.pem");

  and, inside `koWifToken`, under `lib.optionalString useWifTpm`:

    export OPENSSL_MODULES=${pkgs.tpm2-openssl}/lib/ossl-modules
    export TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI=device:/dev/tpmrm0

  `wifCredentialConfig` now passes `"--key" wifKeyFile` instead of the literal
  `wif.pem` path. Nothing else in the credential config moved.

**`tests/wif-tpm.sh` (new, +220)** — this task's verification.

    ./tests/wif-tpm.sh [key-path]            # or $KO_WIF_TPM_KEY
        # 8 checks, "ok N - …" / "FAIL N - …" / "skip N - …", exit 0 iff all pass.
        # Resolves openssl AND tpm2-openssl from ONE source — this flake's
        # homeConfigurations.<host>.pkgs first, nixpkgs# as the fallback — because a
        # provider built against a different OpenSSL will not load into the binary.
        # Skips the TPM half on a host with no TPM; skips the wiring half with no nix.

## Verification

(filled in below)
EOF
echo written

# Handoff: Part A item 2 — shiori's device WIF key is in the TPM

## 1. Objective
This phase did Part A **item 2 only**: move shiori's device WIF signing key off
the filesystem and into the TPM, publish its JWK alongside the old one, prove
decryption with it, and run experiment 2a-removal. Spec:
`/home/sauyon/devel/reports/Homelab secrets bootstrap trust root.md`, Part A
(A1 #1, A6.5, A8). The next phase does **item 3** — enroll utsuho, setsuna,
kyuusaku, fujiwara-user and mari (system + user) — then re-checks the item 4
migration gate.

## 2. State
(filled in at the end of the phase — see the final version)

## 3. Decisions + rationale

- `[agent]` **Mechanism: the nixpkgs `tpm2-openssl` PROVIDER, not tpm2-pkcs11.**
  Probed both on shiori before choosing. The provider needs exactly two exports
  in the `ko-wif-token` wrapper — `OPENSSL_MODULES` and `TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI` — and
  nothing else: no token database, no `tpm2_ptool init`, no PIN, no state
  outside the key file. It also keeps the signer on stdlib + openssl, which is
  the constraint that made it a python script rather than a Go binary. Measured:
  `genpkey -provider tpm2 -algorithm EC -pkeyopt group:P-256` writes a TSS2
  blob, `pkey -pubout` yields the same SubjectPublicKeyInfo the JWK code already
  parsed, `dgst -sha256 -sign` takes 0.18 s, and the signature verifies under the
  default provider alone. No `drovr ask`: the brief reserved one for the case
  where both are viable, and tpm2-pkcs11 is viable only at a much higher price.
- `[agent]` **The signer decides per key, by sniffing the PEM header** (`key_args`),
  not by a flag. A flag would have to be threaded through the credential config,
  `device-test.sh` and every interactive invocation in the same commit, and a
  host whose key moved into the TPM would break at whichever one was missed.
  The header is unambiguous: tpm2-openssl writes `-----BEGIN TSS2 PRIVATE KEY-----`
  and nothing else does.
- `[agent]` **`-provider default` is named a second time, deliberately.** Naming
  any provider on an openssl command line switches the implicit default one off,
  taking the digest and the encoders with it. Dropping the apparent redundancy
  breaks signing.
- `[agent]` **`openssl ec` -> `openssl pkey`** for the public half: `ec` is the
  legacy EC-only command and the TPM key comes out of the provider's generic
  store loader. Checked for drift on the file path — shiori's file key still
  produces kid `REDACTED`, the one already

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

  **1. The plaintext file key is still live and still authorised — the change's headline security property is not achieved, and the test asserts that it is.** `tests/wif-tpm.sh:5-11`, `install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh:125-126`
  
  Measured on this host right now:
  - `~/.config/ko/wif.pem` still exists, mode 0600, plaintext P-256, kid `REDACTED`.
  - The live JWKS at `https://storage.googleapis.com/ko-keys-sauyon/hosts/.well-known/jwks.json` contains three kids, and `01HB4BTt8_…` is one of them. The TPM key's kid `FuJZ9XEZl7_0-…` is another.
  
  So after this change ships, shiori has **two** valid device identities and one of them is a file anyone who reads it once can use forever from anywhere — exactly the threat the header comment at tpm-keygen.sh:6-9 says the TPM upgrade removes. Meanwhile tests/wif-tpm.sh:7 asserts as its rationale #1: "The private half stops being a file." It does not. The test passes anyway because it only ever looks at `wif-tpm.pem`.
  
  Keeping the old kid published *during* the switch is correct (tpm-keygen.sh:125-126 says so, and it is right). The bug is that there is no step 5 and no check anywhere: nothing in the diff shreds `~/.config/ko/wif.pem`, nothing republishes the JWKS without `01HB4BTt8_…`, and nothing in `tests/wif-tpm.sh` will ever go red while both exist. Failure scenario: you switch, the tests say "all good", you consider item 2 done, and the plaintext key sits there indefinitely with full KMS decrypt authority.
  
  Concretely needed: a step 5 in tpm-keygen.sh's Next block ("after `hms` succeeds: `shred -u ~/.config/ko/wif.pem` and rerun admin-setup.sh with only the surviving JWKs"), plus a check in tests/wif-tpm.sh that FAILs while `~/.config/ko/wif.pem` exists or while its kid is in the JWKS. (Also note: `~/.config/ko/experiment/wif.pem`, referenced by device-keygen.sh:9 and device-test.sh:6, is a separate stale artefact — it's currently absent here, but it's the same hazard class.)
  
  ---
  
  ## IMPORTANT
  
  **2. `tests/wif-tpm.sh` exits 0 when every substantive check has skipped.** `tests/wif-tpm.sh:40`, `:117-118`, `:127-128`, `:163-164`, `:200-201`, `:219-220`
  
  `skip()` increments `n` but never `fails`, and the exit status is `[ "$fails" = 0 ]`. There is no "all checks skipped" guard. Four independent conditions each silently delete a whole block:
  
  - `:117` — `[ ! -e "${tcti#device:}" ]` skips *all* TPM checks. This also fires for any non-`device:` TCTI (`swtpm:…`, `tabrmd`), where `${tcti#device:}` is the whole string and never a path.
  - `:127` — `[ -z "$OPENSSL_MODULES" ]` skips checks 2-5. `OPENSSL_MODULES` comes from `pick` at :60, which is `nix build` — offline, or with a flake eval error, `prov_root` is empty and the TPM JWK/sign/JWKS checks all vanish. Note this is precisely the variable check 8 exists to assert, so the test skips on the condition it is meant to catch.
  - `:163` — offline ⇒ the JWKS membership check skips. That is the only check in the suite that would catch an RFC 7638 kid regression (see finding 6).
  - `:200` — see finding 3.
  
  Failure scenario: run on a laptop with no network and a cold nix store. Output: `skip … / skip … / ok (file-key path) / skip …` → `4 checks, all good`, exit 0, having proved nothing about the TPM. Fix: track `skips` and either exit non-zero, or at minimum require ≥1 non-skipped TPM check when a key file is present.
  
  **3. Dropping shiori from `wifHosts` — the exact regression the wiring check exists for — produces a SKIP, not a FAIL.** `tests/wif-tpm.sh:195-201`
  
  If `wifHosts = []`, `nix eval` still succeeds and returns `/home/sauyon/.config/sops/gcp-key.json` (home.nix:1503). `nix build .#…activationPackage` at :199 then cannot make that path exist. I checked: `~/.config/sops/` contains only `age-unused.txt` and a zero-byte `gcp-key.json.tmp` — **`gcp-key.json` does not exist on this host**. So `[ ! -e "$cfg" ]` is true, `:201` fires `skip "no realisable credential config for $host (unenrolled host?)"`, both checks 7 and 8 disappear, and the suite exits 0. Same outcome if `wifTpmHosts = []` is combined with removing the host from `wifHosts`. The `(unenrolled host?)` wording actively encourages you to shrug it off. Fix: since `$host` is known to be enrolled (you just checked its TSS2 key), a non-store `$cfg` should be a `bad`, not a `skip` — e.g. `case "$cfg" in /nix/store/*) … ;; *) bad "credential config is not a store path: $cfg" ;; esac`.
  
  **4. The `TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI=device:/dev/null` check proves something weaker than it claims, and the comment overclaims.** `tests/wif-tpm.sh:146-155`
  
  Measured: with `TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI=device:/dev/null`, openssl never reaches the key at all —
  ```
  ERROR:tcti:…Tss2_Tcti_Device_Init() Failed to read response header fd 3
  pkey: unable to load provider tpm2
  ```
  It fails at **provider initialisation**. The signer dies in `pub_xy` on the very first `openssl pkey`, before any signing. So the check demonstrates "the tpm2 provider needs a working TCTI" — a property of the provider, not of this key blob. It would pass identically for a TSS2 blob wrapped to a *different* TPM, and it would pass identically if `OPENSSL_MODULES` were garbage.
  
  It does still discriminate file-key vs TSS2 (I confirmed the file key at `~/.config/ko/wif.pem` signs happily with `TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI=device:/dev/null`, rc=0, because `key_args` returns `[]` for it). But that discrimination flows from exactly the same first-line sniff as check 1 at :124-125, so the two checks are one piece of evidence, not two. The comment at :146-148 ("A key that still signs there was never in the TPM" / "the TCTI layer opens it and the command reaches nothing") describes a mechanism that does not occur. Additionally the check accepts *any* non-zero exit, so a broken `$signer` path or an unreadable key also reads as success. Fix: assert on the failure text (`grep -q 'unable to load provider tpm2\|tcti'`), or better, exercise the real claim — sign under `TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI=device:/dev/tpmrm0` with the TPM's *owner hierarchy* unavailable, or at minimum stop the header from claiming it proves TPM residency.
  
  **5. A JWK-print failure after `mv` leaves a half-enrolled host with no recovery hint.** `install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh:108-113`
  
  Order is: `chmod 400` → `mv "$tmpd/key" "$out"` → **then** `KO_OPENSSL="$OSSL" python3 "$repo/home/scripts/ko-wif-token.py" --key "$out" --jwk | tee "$jwk"`. With `set -euo pipefail`, any failure of that last line aborts with the key already installed. And that line is the one place in the script that uses a **bare `python3` from `$PATH`** while everything else (`$OSSL`, `$OPENSSL_MODULES`) is an absolute nix path — on a freshly-installed host (the intended audience) `python3` may not be on PATH at all. Then: `~/.config/ko/wif-tpm.pem` exists, no JWK was printed, and re-running gives `exists, refusing to overwrite` with the only advice being "move it aside" (i.e. throw away a perfectly good TPM key). The obvious recovery — just run ko-wif-token.py `--jwk` against the installed key — is never mentioned. Fix: emit the JWK from `$tmpd/key` *before* the `mv`, and/or add the recovery line to the refuse-to-overwrite message at :42.
  
  **6. The RFC 7638 thumbprint is never independently recomputed — the only check that covers it is network-gated.** `home/scripts/ko-wif-token.py:69-74`, `tests/wif-tpm.sh:108-112`, `:131-134`, `:160-169`
  
  `roundtrip` recomputes `x||y` independently via `openssl pkey | tail -c 64` (good), but nothing recomputes `sha256(json({crv,kty,x,y}, sorted))`. Check 2 only asserts `len(kid) == 43`. The JWT header's `kid` comes from the same `jwk()` call as `--jwk`, so the two can never disagree. The single check that would catch a thumbprint regression is :165 against the live JWKS — which `skip`s offline (finding 2). The brief's invariant "the JWK printed for a key must describe the key that actually signs" is therefore half-tested: the point is verified, the kid is not. Failure scenario: someone "tidies" `jwk()` to hash the full dict including `alg`/`use`, or drops `sort_keys=True`. Run the suite offline: 7 ok, 1 skip, exit 0. Deploy: STS 401 on every token, minutes later, with nothing local to explain it. Fix: a four-line independent thumbprint in the test's python (it's stdlib).
  
  **7. `pick`'s `.#` is cwd-relative, so the "one source" invariant both comments assert is unenforced.** `tests/wif-tpm.sh:45-60`, `install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh:54-73`
  
  `nix build ".#homeConfigurations.$host.pkgs.openssl"` resolves `.` against the cwd. I verified nix *does* search upward to the enclosing git root (works from `install/wif/`), but from outside the repo (`/tmp`, `$HOME`) it errors with `could not find a flake.nix file` and the `pick` fallback silently takes `nixpkgs#openssl` / `nixpkgs#tpm2-openssl` from the registry — a different nixpkgs revision than the flake. tests/wif-tpm.sh:25 explicitly promises "Run it from anywhere; paths are resolved against the repo this file lives in", which is false for the only part that matters (the `nix eval` at :195 *does* `cd "$repo"`; `pick` does not).
  
  Worse, `pick` is called twice independently: it is possible to get `ossl_root` from the flake and `prov_root` from registry nixpkgs (or vice versa), which is precisely the mixed pair both comments warn about — "the error names neither". Nothing detects this. Fix: `(cd "$repo" && nix build …)` inside `pick`, and resolve both from the same source or fail.
  
  ---
  
  ## nit
  
  - **`install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh:26` vs `home.nix:48`** — the generator honours `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, the consumer hardcodes `${homeDirectory}/.config`. With `XDG_CONFIG_HOME=~/.cfg` the key lands where home.nix will never look; sops-nix then fails at activation with `No such file or directory`. (Pre-existing pattern from device-keygen.sh:7, but newly relevant.)
  - **`install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh:46-48`** — `dev="${tcti#device:}"` assumes a `device:` TCTI. For `swtpm:…`/`tabrmd` the script hard-exits with `no TPM at swtpm:host=… (set TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI to point elsewhere)` — the message tells you to do the thing that just broke it.
  - **`install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh:34-36`** — `$repo` comes from logical `cd`+`pwd` but `$out` is run through `realpath -m`. If the repo is reached via a symlinked prefix (`~/dotfiles -> ~/devel/dotfiles`), the two never share a prefix and the "don't write the key inside the repo" guard is bypassed. Also `case` treats `$repo` as a glob pattern.
  - **`home/scripts/ko-wif-token.py:41-48`** — `f.readline()` on a file with no newline reads the whole file into memory (point `--key` at a multi-GB blob → OOM). And the sniff looks only at line 1: a TSS2 PEM with a leading blank or comment line (which openssl itself tolerates) takes the file-key branch and then fails with the *wrong* hint ("generate one with: openssl ecparam …"). tpm-keygen.sh:88 guarantees the header is on line 1 for keys it produces, so this only bites hand-edited files.
  - **`home/scripts/ko-wif-token.py:55,63-66`** — `pkey` accepts non-EC keys where `ec` did not. A P-384/P-521 key survives the `der[-65:]` / `pt[0] == 4` guard roughly 1 time in 256 and yields a silently wrong 32/32 split. Pre-existing risk (`ec` also accepted P-384), but the guard is now the *only* type check. Cheap fix: assert `len(der) == 91`.
  - **`home/scripts/ko-wif-token.py:97,101`** — the key file is stat'd/read four times per token (`key_args` twice, plus two openssl invocations), and `sign()` re-derives the kid via a full `openssl pkey` TPM read. Harmless (0.4s measured) but means the header `kid` and the signature come from two separate reads of a file that could, in principle, differ.
  - **`home.nix:57-59`** — "must be tpm2-openssl built against THIS openssl, or the module refuses to load" overstates what nix enforces. `nix-store -q --references` on `…tpm2-openssl-1.3.0` lists only glibc, tpm2-tss and itself; `tpm2.so`'s RUNPATH is `tpm2-tss/lib:glibc/lib` with **no** openssl entry — it resolves `libcrypto.so.3` out of the loading process. So the pairing is a build-time header dependency only, nothing pins it at runtime, and any ABI-compatible OpenSSL 3.x would load it. Nothing breaks today (both come from the same `pkgs`), but the comment claims an invariant that neither nix nor any check enforces.
  - **`tests/wif-tpm.sh:209-210`** — check 8 greps the wrapper *text* for `OPENSSL_MODULES=` / `TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI=`. It never checks that the exported directory exists or contains `tpm2.so`. Replace `pkgs.tpm2-openssl` with any derivation lacking `lib/ossl-modules` and the check still passes.
  - **`tests/wif-tpm.sh:97,108`** — the suite never invokes the production wrapper for signing; it reproduces the env by hand. (I confirmed separately that `env -i …/bin/ko-wif-token --adc` works end to end, including `clock_ok` via `/usr/bin/timedatectl`, so this is a coverage gap, not a live bug.) Also :108's `--jwk` output isn't error-checked — a failure there surfaces as the misleading "the JWK x||y is not this key's public point".
  - **`tests/wif-tpm.sh:124-125`** — `head -1` comparison is CRLF-sensitive.
  - **`tests/wif-tpm.sh:52` / `install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh:61`** — unquoted `$(nix build …)` in `for` is deliberate (multi-output: openssl's `outputsToInstall` is `["bin","man"]`, and `pick` correctly picks the `bin` one — verified) but leaves globbing on. Store path names admit `?` and `+`; with no `nullglob` an unmatched glob passes through unchanged, so this is theoretical only.
  - **`install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh:88`** — `head -1 … | grep -qx …` under `pipefail` is racy in principle (grep exits on match → SIGPIPE → head 141 → pipeline 141 → false "not a TPM key blob"). On a 394-byte file `head` has written and exited long before; effectively zero risk, but `grep -qx … < <(head -1 …)` costs nothing.
  - **`tests/wif-tpm.sh`** is not referenced from README.md (which documents only `tests/hyprlock-faillock.sh`) or from any CI. Its only entry point is step 4 of tpm-keygen.sh's output.
  
  ---
  
  ## Do the tests exercise the behaviour, or merely pass?
  
  **Partly exercise, with three named holes.** Checks 3 and 6 are real end-to-end work: a JWT is signed (through the TPM for check 3), the DER is reconstructed by independent code, and openssl verifies it against the key's own public half and against the JWK's `x||y`. Check 7 reads the *evaluated* credential config out of the nix store rather than the source text, which is the right altitude. Check 5 hits the live JWKS. Those four would genuinely go red on the regressions they name.
  
  The holes:
  1. **Nothing would go red for finding 1** — the suite has no concept of the old file key, so the migration's whole point can be unfinished and the suite still says "all good".
  2. **`skip` is indistinguishable from `ok` in the exit status** (finding 2), and two of the skips fire on exactly the conditions their block exists to detect (findings 2 and 3). Offline + cold store ⇒ a green run that proved one thing (the file-key path).
  3. **The negative TPM check is theatre in its stated form** (finding 4): it re-derives its discriminating power from the same `head -1` sniff as check 1, and the mechanism its comment describes is not the mechanism that fires.
  
  On the "test and code share a bug" question specifically: `raw2der` vs `der_sig_to_raw` is genuinely independent; `tail -c 64` vs `der[-65:]` is genuinely independent; **the RFC 7638 thumbprint is not** (finding 6), and the `key_args` header sniff is the single shared signal behind both check 1 and check 4 (finding 4).

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for the TPM-resident device WIF key (report A1 #1, A6.5, Part A item 2).
#
# Moving the device key into the TPM changes three things that matter and must
# not change a fourth:
#
#   1. The private half stops being a file THAT STILL WORKS. `~/.config/ko/wif.pem`
#      is a P-256 private key in plaintext on disk -- anyone who reads it once can
#      mint device JWTs forever, from anywhere, and the only evidence is a KMS
#      access log entry that looks exactly like shiori. Generating a TPM key does
#      not fix that; only removing the old key's kid from the published JWKS does,
#      because the JWKS is what grants authority. So the last check here computes
#      the old file key's kid and requires it to be ABSENT from the live JWKS. It
#      is meant to stay red through the migration and go green when the old
#      identity is revoked -- the step it would otherwise be easy to call done.
#   2. The new key cannot sign without a working TPM connection. Pointing the TCTI
#      at a device that is not a TPM must make signing fail. Read that check for
#      exactly what it proves: it fails inside provider initialisation, so it
#      shows the TPM key's signing path goes through the chip, NOT that this blob
#      is bound to THIS chip specifically -- a blob wrapped to a different TPM
#      would fail here identically. Proving the latter needs a second TPM.
#   3. The JWK the signer publishes still describes the key that signs. The kid is
#      an RFC 7638 thumbprint over x/y, so a mismatch means the JWKS entry
#      authorises a key nobody holds and STS rejects every token -- a failure that
#      only shows up against Google, minutes later, as a 401. Both halves are
#      recomputed here independently of the signer: the point from openssl, the
#      thumbprint from hashlib.
#   4. The file-key path keeps working untouched. mari is darwin and has no TPM,
#      and the other four hosts are not enrolled yet, so the file path is still
#      the one most of the fleet boots on. It is exercised with no provider
#      environment at all, which is how those hosts run it.
#
# A skip is NOT a pass. On a host that has a TPM and a key, anything that stops
# this file from checking the TPM is a failure of the test, not an exemption:
# `needed` marks those, and the exit status counts them. Only genuinely external
# conditions (no TPM on this host, no network, no nix) stay soft skips.
#
#   ./tests/wif-tpm.sh                        # default key path
#   ./tests/wif-tpm.sh ~/.config/ko/wif-tpm.pem
#
# Run it from anywhere; every nix invocation below runs with the cwd inside the
# repo this file lives in, so `.#` resolves to THIS flake and not to whatever
# flake the caller happened to be standing in.
set -u

repo="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
signer="$repo/home/scripts/ko-wif-token.py"
host="$(uname -n)"; host="${host%%.*}"
key="${1:-${KO_WIF_TPM_KEY:-$HOME/.config/ko/wif-tpm.pem}}"
oldkey="${KO_WIF_FILE_KEY:-$HOME/.config/ko/wif.pem}"
tcti="${TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI:-device:/dev/tpmrm0}"
issuer="https://storage.googleapis.com/ko-keys-sauyon/hosts"

fails=0; n=0; skipped=0
ok()   { n=$((n+1)); printf 'ok %d - %s\n' "$n" "$1"; }
bad()  { n=$((n+1)); fails=$((fails+1)); printf 'FAIL %d - %s\n' "$n" "$1"; }
skip() { n=$((n+1)); skipped=$((skipped+1)); printf 'skip %d - %s\n' "$n" "$1"; }
# A condition that should be impossible on a host this file is meant to run on.
# Skipping here would mean reporting "all good" for a run that checked nothing.
needed() { bad "$1"$'\n'"      (this host has a TPM and a device key, so this is a broken test run, not a skip)"; }
is()   { if [ "$2" = "$3" ]; then ok "$1"; else bad "$1"$'\n'"      want: $3"$'\n'"      got:  $2"; fi; }

work=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT

# openssl and the tpm2 provider have to come from ONE source: a provider built
# against a different OpenSSL than the binary loading it may refuse to load, and
# the error names neither. Prefer this flake's own pkgs, because that is the pair
# home.nix wires into ko-wif-token; fall back to plain nixpkgs for a host with no
# homeConfiguration. The `cd "$repo"` is load-bearing -- `.#` is resolved against
# the CWD, so without it a run from outside the repo silently takes the registry's
# nixpkgs for one of the two and this flake's for the other.
pick() { # pick <relative path> <flake attr>... -> first out path that contains it
  local p attr
  for attr in "${@:2}"; do
    for p in $(cd "$repo" && nix build --no-link --print-out-paths "$attr" 2>/dev/null); do
      [ -e "$p/$1" ] && { printf '%s\n' "$p"; return 0; }
    done
  done
  return 1
}
ossl_root=$(pick bin/openssl ".#homeConfigurations.$host.pkgs.openssl" "nixpkgs#openssl")
prov_root=$(pick lib/ossl-modules/tpm2.so ".#homeConfigurations.$host.pkgs.tpm2-openssl" "nixpkgs#tpm2-openssl")
OSSL="${ossl_root:+$ossl_root/bin/openssl}"
[ -n "$OSSL" ] || OSSL=$(command -v openssl)
[ -n "$OSSL" ] || { echo "need openssl (nixpkgs#openssl)" >&2; exit 1; }

# The signer resolves openssl from KO_OPENSSL and the tpm2 provider from the
# ambient OPENSSL_MODULES, exactly as the home.nix wrapper sets them.
export KO_OPENSSL="$OSSL"
[ -n "$prov_root" ] && export OPENSSL_MODULES="$prov_root/lib/ossl-modules"
export TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI="$tcti"

# JWS ES256 carries the signature as raw r||s; openssl verifies DER. Converting
# it here rather than reusing the signer's own der_sig_to_raw is the point: a bug
# shared by signer and test would verify against itself and prove nothing.
raw2der() { # raw2der <base64url sig> -> DER on stdout
  python3 - "$1" <<'PY'
import sys, base64
s = sys.argv[1]
raw = base64.urlsafe_b64decode(s + "=" * (-len(s) % 4))
if len(raw) != 64:
    sys.exit(f"expected a 64-byte raw ECDSA signature, got {len(raw)}")
def i(b):
    b = b.lstrip(b"\0") or b"\0"
    if b[0] & 0x80:
        b = b"\0" + b
    return b"\x02" + bytes([len(b)]) + b
body = i(raw[:32]) + i(raw[32:])
sys.stdout.buffer.write(b"\x30" + bytes([len(body)]) + body)

}

# The kid of <key>, recomputed from scratch: RFC 7638 is sha256 over the compact,
# key-sorted JSON of exactly {crv,kty,x,y}. Deriving it here from the PUBLIC POINT
# rather than from the signer's own JWK is what makes it evidence -- reusing
# jwk()["kid"] would only prove the signer agrees with itself.
kid_of_point() { # kid_of_point <64-byte x||y, base64 std> -> kid
  python3 - "$1" <<'PY'
import sys, base64, hashlib, json
pt = base64.b64decode(sys.argv[1])
if len(pt) != 64:
    sys.exit(f"expected a 64-byte public point, got {len(pt)}")
u = lambda b: base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()
j = {"crv": "P-256", "kty": "EC", "x": u(pt[:32]), "y": u(pt[32:])}
print(u(hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(j, separators=(",", ":"), sort_keys=True).encode()).digest()))

point_of() { # point_of <key> [openssl provider args...] -> 64-byte x||y, base64 std
  # SubjectPublicKeyInfo for P-256 is 91 bytes ending in the x||y point.
  "$OSSL" pkey "${@:2}" -in "$1" -pubout -outform DER 2>/dev/null | tail -c 64 | base64 | tr -d '\n'

# Sign a JWT with <key>, then check it against the public half the signer itself
# published as a JWK. Silent on success; prints the reason and returns non-zero
# otherwise.
roundtrip() { # roundtrip <key> [openssl provider args...]

          --aud test-aud --skip-clock-check 2>&1) || { echo "sign failed: $jwt"; return 1; }
  msg=${jwt%.*}; sig=${jwt##*.}

    || { echo "could not extract the public key: $(tail -1 "$work/e")"; return 1; }

    >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "the signature did not verify against the key's own public half"; return 1; }

  # that died here would be reported as a point mismatch, which is a different bug.
  jwkjson=$(python3 "$signer" --key "$k" --jwk 2>&1) || { echo "--jwk failed: $(printf '%s' "$jwkjson" | tail -1)"; return 1; }
  jwkpoint=$(printf '%s' "$jwkjson" | python3 -c 'import json, sys, base64
j = json.load(sys.stdin)
u = lambda s: base64.urlsafe_b64decode(s + "==")
sys.stdout.write(base64.b64encode(u(j["x"]) + u(j["y"])).decode())') || { echo "unparseable JWK"; return 1; }
  [ "$jwkpoint" = "$point" ] || { echo "the JWK x||y is not this key's public point"; return 1; }
  return 0
}

have_tpm=0; [ -e "${tcti#device:}" ] && have_tpm=1
have_key=0; [ -r "$key" ] && have_key=1

# ── the TPM key ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if [ "$have_tpm" = 0 ]; then
  skip "TPM key checks: no TPM at ${tcti#device:} (this host has none, or set TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI)"
elif [ "$have_key" = 0 ]; then
  bad "the device key exists and is TPM-resident"$'\n'"      $key is missing or unreadable; generate it with ./install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh"
else
  # A TSS2 PRIVATE KEY is the wrapped-blob format tpm2-openssl writes. A plain
  # "EC PRIVATE KEY" here would mean the key never left the filesystem.
  is "the device key is a TSS2 (TPM-wrapped) private key, not an EC file key" \
     "$(head -1 "$key" | tr -d '\r')" "-----BEGIN TSS2 PRIVATE KEY-----"

  if [ -z "${OPENSSL_MODULES:-}" ]; then
    # Not a skip: this is the very thing check "ko-wif-token exports ..." asserts
    # the wrapper provides, so quietly passing without it would be circular.
    needed "the tpm2 openssl provider is available (nixpkgs#tpm2-openssl)"
  else
    j=$(python3 "$signer" --key "$key" --jwk 2>&1)
    if printf '%s' "$j" | python3 -c 'import json, sys
j = json.load(sys.stdin)
assert j["kty"] == "EC" and j["crv"] == "P-256" and j["alg"] == "ES256", j
assert len(j["kid"]) == 43 and len(j["x"]) == 43 and len(j["y"]) == 43, j' 2>/dev/null; then
      ok "ko-wif-token prints a well-formed P-256 JWK for the TPM key"
    else
      bad "ko-wif-token prints a well-formed P-256 JWK for the TPM key"$'\n'"$(printf '%s' "$j" | tail -3 | sed 's/^/      /')"
    fi

    if err=$(roundtrip "$key" -provider tpm2 -provider default); then
      ok "a JWT signed by the TPM key verifies against the JWK ko-wif-token publishes"
    else
      bad "a JWT signed by the TPM key verifies against the JWK ko-wif-token publishes"$'\n'"      $err"
    fi

    # The kid, recomputed from the public point. Without this, nothing in the
    # suite would notice jwk() hashing the wrong field set or dropping
    # sort_keys -- the JWT header and --jwk both come from that one function, so
    # they agree with each other however wrong they are, and the only other
    # witness (the live JWKS) is network-gated.
    want_kid=$(printf '%s' "$j" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["kid"])' 2>/dev/null)
    got_kid=$(kid_of_point "$(point_of "$key" -provider tpm2 -provider default)" 2>/dev/null)
    if [ -n "$got_kid" ]; then
      is "the kid is the RFC 7638 thumbprint of {crv,kty,x,y}" "$want_kid" "$got_kid"
    else
      needed "the kid is the RFC 7638 thumbprint of {crv,kty,x,y} (could not recompute it)"
    fi

    # failure text is asserted because "any non-zero exit" would also be
    # satisfied by a typo in $signer or an unreadable key -- a pass for the
    # wrong reason, in the one check whose whole job is to be a negative.
    out=$(TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI="device:/dev/null" python3 "$signer" --key "$key" \
            --iss "$issuer" --sub "device:$host" --aud test-aud --skip-clock-check 2>&1)

      bad "the TPM key's signing path goes through the TPM"$'\n'"      it signed with TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI=device:/dev/null"
    elif printf '%s' "$out" | grep -qiE 'provider|tcti|tpm'; then
      ok "the TPM key's signing path goes through the TPM (a dead TCTI refuses it)"
    else

    fi

    # idea for the device tier. A key configured but not published is a host that
    # boots to an STS 401, and nothing local can tell you that.
    kid=$(printf '%s' "$j" | python3 -c 'import json, sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["kid"])' 2>/dev/null)

      needed "JWKS membership: no kid to look for (the JWK check above failed)"

      skip "JWKS membership: $issuer is unreachable"
    elif printf '%s' "$jwks" | grep -qF "$kid"; then
      ok "the TPM key's kid is published in the live JWKS"
    else
      bad "the TPM key's kid is published in the live JWKS"$'\n'"      $kid is not in $issuer/.well-known/jwks.json"$'\n'"      publish it from the admin host (install/wif/admin-setup.sh)"
